What to know about the Iran war today:
- At least 20 people, including a U.S. national, have been killed in a week of Houthi on Saudi Arabia's main airport, pushing oil prices back up and prompting President Trump to consider joining the Saudi-led battle against the Houthis in Yemen as it becomes the epicenter of the .
- The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, climbed back to a two-week high over $105 a barrel Monday after President Trump said Saturday that he was considering whether to join Saudi Arabia's offensive against the Houthis in Yemen.
- Fighting also continues near the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military announced Sunday that it had disabled a cargo vessel after the crew "ignored warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade" of Iran's ports and vessels.
Saudis investigate why deadly strike on Riyadh airport wasn't intercepted
Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday.
The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.
One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 620 miles to reach Riyadh.
Delta delays planned flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid attacks on airports
Delta Air Lines said Monday it is delaying plans for nonstop flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid escalating attacks between Yemen's Houthi militants and Saudi Arabia.
"The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," the company said in a statement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."
its plans to operate nonstop flights to Riyadh three times a week on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft in October 2026. It said at the time that the new destination would help strengthen business and travel ties between the United States and Saudi Arabia.
The company said Monday the launch of Atlanta-Riyadh flights will take place in March 2027.
Iran's foreign ministry says U.K.'s accusations are unfounded
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday denied the U.K.'s allegations that Tehran was involved in last month's security incident at a British base used by American bombers.
In a statement posted to social media, the foreign ministry condemned what it said were "unfounded accusations by the United Kingdom against Iran."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier Monday the security incident at RAF Fairford — which led to the who were later released on bail — was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
In its response, Tehran said by using terms like "highly likely" and "almost" certain, the U.K. is "hiding behind vague language without presenting concrete evidence or proof."
NATO countries issue joint statement on Iran and RAF Fairford security incident
Foreign ministers of NATO member countries on Monday issued a joint statement condemning "Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
The statement said the countries recognize the U.K.'s assertion that last month's , a U.S.-run air base in Britain, was likely coordinated by Iran.
"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the joint statement said. " Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
In a separate statement, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he welcomes the statement issued by allies and partners, echoing their denouncement of "Iran's involvement in violence and threats on Allied territory."
"NATO will continue to do its part to safeguard the security of our one billion people across the Alliance," Rutte said.
Houthis confirm they targeted Riyadh's airport again with ballistic missile
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack targeting Riyadh's international airport on Monday, after a Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down a missile over the capital.
"Our armed forces were able to target (King) Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital Riyadh this evening with a ballistic missile and the hit was precise," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said. He said the group also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone.
Saree also warned against "the consequences of operating flights toward Saudi airports, as they are not safe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the sacred areas in Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah."
It's unclear whether there were any injuries.
CBS/AFP
Multiple blasts heard in Riyadh, as residents warned of aerial threat
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.
Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
U.K. foreign minister announces sanctions against 2 Iranian nationals
U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement.
"We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
Americans detained for photographing attacks in Saudi Arabia, U.S. embassy says
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
Iran denies involvement in U.K. air base incident, state media reports
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
CBS/AFP
Iran claims to have struck 3 supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the last 2 days
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.
The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."
It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."
The statement warned that "any cooperation by commercial vessels and oil tankers with the invading, plundering American terrorist and smuggling army in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf region will be met with a decisive response from us."

articles.title: Saudis vow firm response to attacks testing country's resilience
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia's energy minister vowed a firm response Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks, acknowledging that the kingdom’s infrastructure and resilience have been te...
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister vowed a firm response Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks, acknowledging that the kingdom’s infrastructure and resilience have been tested.
The Houthi attacks over the weekend marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Saudi Arabia has long supported the internationally recognized government.
On Sunday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing one person, just hours after another Houthi-claimed attack on the same site killed 13 people and left hundreds of others wounded, forcing authorities to suspend operations there.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, a regional powerhouse and the world's top oil exporter which has poured billions of dollars into its military, were the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade.
"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience. They have also tested decisions made long before present crises, because resilience is built before crises begin," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," he told a high-profile conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theater of operations for our forces."
Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck the capital's King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.
Air defenses also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. Journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the city Sunday.
"The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighborhood in the city's north.
Authorities extended the suspension of operations at the airport, even as Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season kicks off this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
The airport was not the only one in the country to be targeted: the civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.
"Saudi air defenses have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively."
Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate Sunday.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others.
Saturday's attack on Riyadh drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including U.S. President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was "deeply concerned" over the escalation.
Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died Sunday after being wounded the day before.
Witnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath.
"Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them."
On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counteroffensive against the Houthis around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday.
The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Saudi coalition tackling drones, missiles headed toward kingdom
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said ⁠Monday ⁠it was dealing with drones and missiles heading ⁠toward Saudi Arabia, ​as hostilities with ​the ⁠Iran-aligned ‌Yemeni...

The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said Monday it was dealing with drones and missiles heading toward Saudi Arabia, as hostilities with the Iran-aligned Yemeni group persist.
State-backed broadcaster Al Ekhbariya reported that the military coalition was responding to a missile and drone threat but did not specify where the projectiles were headed.
"The coalition is currently dealing with a threat involving drones and cruise missiles targeting the kingdom," the broadcaster said.
The latest report of attacks comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.
On Sunday afternoon, an unidentified projectile struck King Khalid International Airport's Terminal 4 in Riyadh, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi-led coalition also said it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
A day earlier, on Saturday, a Houthi attack struck a passenger terminal at the airport, killing 13 people and injuring 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out Saturday's attack and described the strike as a "full-fledged war crime."

articles.full_text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, according to Interia, rejected an Israeli offer of military assistance in fighting Yemen’s Houthis, conveyed through the United States. The outlet cites a diplomatic source of the Haaretz newspaper. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to this information, seeks to use the situation to move closer to Riyadh.
Contacts through the United States
Israel and Saudi Arabia have no official diplomatic relations, but cooperate to a limited extent on security issues. In September, Israeli media reported that, at Riyadh’s request, Israel began transmitting intelligence through the United States to protect the kingdom’s strategic infrastructure from Houthi attacks.
According to Haaretz’s diplomatic source, bin Salman did not agree to the offer due to fears of a negative reaction from Saudi society to military cooperation with Israel. Netanyahu views such interaction as an opportunity to bring closer the normalization of relations between the two states.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Normalization conditions and attacks
Riyadh links a possible understanding with Israel to progress in the establishment of a Palestinian state. US President Donald Trump is seeking Saudi Arabia’s accession to the Abraham Accords, concluded in 2020 at Washington’s initiative. Under these agreements, Israel established diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and later Morocco.
Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition that intervened in the war in Yemen against the Iran-backed Houthis after they seized the capital and drove out the internationally recognized government. In recent days, the Houthis have intensified attacks on the kingdom: during Saturday’s shelling of the airport in Riyadh, 12 people were killed and another 309 were injured, according to Interia.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia low on interceptor missiles amid Houthi attacks - The Siasat Daily
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia low on interceptor missiles amid Houthi attacks  The Siasat Daily
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptor missiles needed to defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, raising concerns over the kingdom’s ability to protect critical infrastructure as hostilities intensify, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.
Saudi officials said supplies of interceptors needed to repel further strikes were running low as the Houthis stepped up attacks on airports and energy facilities. The shortage has added pressure on the kingdom’s air defences as it faces threats across its vast territory.
Crown prince moves between fortified palaces
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers and is accompanied by a handpicked security team, the WSJ reported, citing officials familiar with his movements.
The 41-year-old crown prince’s last public appearance was on Tuesday, October 6, when he donated blood as part of a national campaign, according to the report.
Saudi Arabia has been repositioning its air-defence batteries to prioritise the protection of royal palaces and energy infrastructure. The Houthis have targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh at least four times, the WSJ reported, adding to concerns about the security of the kingdom’s aviation network.
Riyadh airport attacks kill 14
The latest airport attacks came amid an escalation in hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. The two attacks on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, October 10, and Sunday, October 11, killed a combined 14 people and injured hundreds, according to Saudi authorities.
Saturday’s attack killed 13 people and injured 309, while Sunday’s separate strike caused a fire at Terminal 4, killing one person and injuring 11 others.
The attacks form part of a wider Houthi campaign against Saudi infrastructure, which the group says is retaliation for Saudi actions against it.
The confrontation has intensified since July, when Saudi-led coalition forces struck Sanaa International Airport in Yemen. The strike targeted the airport’s operational runway amid efforts to prevent a flight carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi targets.
The group has also targeted energy infrastructure, including Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, and threatened shipping routes in the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia seeks additional air defences
Riyadh has approached Pakistan, a key military ally, for assistance and is searching internationally for additional air-defence systems, the WSJ reported. Saudi Arabia is also considering recruiting foreign fighters to support its Yemeni allies.
Despite Crown Prince Mohammed’s efforts to strengthen ties with US President Donald Trump, Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for military assistance to reverse the Houthi advance, although it has sent military advisers, according to the newspaper.
Trump said over the weekend that the United States was communicating with the Houthis and might join Saudi strikes against the group.
Saudi Arabia is also exploring diplomatic options to contain the conflict. However, military action risks drawing the kingdom deeper into an asymmetric conflict in which the Houthis have demonstrated their ability to inflict significant damage.
Oil exports and Vision 2030 under pressure
The escalating attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s oil-export routes, particularly the East-West pipeline, which transports crude across the country to the Red Sea and provides an alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
A Houthi attack on the pipeline in September and threats to Red Sea shipping have put this alternative route at risk. The group announced a maritime blockade targeting Saudi Arabia in July, while its advance along Yemen’s coast near the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint has increased concerns about shipping through the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The conflict is also adding to the challenges facing Crown Prince Mohammed’s Vision 2030 programme, which aims to reduce the kingdom’s dependence on oil by expanding tourism, attracting foreign investment and developing new industries.
Rising defence and infrastructure costs threaten to divert funds from major development projects. Several initiatives, including NEOM, have been stalled or placed under review, while Saudi Arabia must still finance Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup.
Foreign investment fell during the first two quarters of the year and remained below the crown prince’s 2030 target, according to the WSJ report. Capital Economics also recorded a contraction in the non-oil economy between the first and second quarters.
The Saudi Finance Ministry expects gross domestic product to shrink by 3.6 per cent in 2026, according to the report.
The escalating Houthi attacks have added to the challenges facing Saudi Arabia as it seeks to protect its oil-export routes and pursue its economic diversification plans amid the Iran war.

articles.title: Why are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia and how are they breaching its air defences? - The Independent
articles.summary: Why are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia and how are they breaching its air defences?  The Independent
articles.full_text:

Yemen’s Houthi rebels have launched a lightning offensive across the country's Red Sea coast, seizing control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and threatening to expand the frozen US-Israeli conflict with Iran to the east.
The land grab has been backed by a deadly campaign of deep strikes inside the kingdom. Over the weekend, Houthi missile and drone attacks struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 13 people — marking the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.
By securing a position overlooking the narrow Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Iran-aligned group has opened a second pressure point, further squeezing Saudi Arabia’s oil exports already diverted from the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts say the main aim of the offensive is to secure control over the Red Sea as Iran maintains its grip over Hormuz, allowing them to raise oil prices and making it harder for Washington to resolve the crisis.
Gulf states – already deliberating over Iran’s ambitions to control shipping through Hormuz – will have to choose between tolerating the status quo and engaging with Tehran to protect trade across the region, they say.
Already fighting a deeply unpopular war to the east, Donald Trump has avoided any commitment to bailing ally Saudi Arabia out with strikes against the Houthis, though experts say US intervention may be needed to break the Houthi grip on the Red Sea.
The Independent looks at how the Houthis are advancing, and what this means for regional stability.
Why are the Houthis fighting with Saudi Arabia?
The Houthi rebels are a military, political and religious movement that rules over most of northwest Yemen and has disrupted global trade and energy markets with strikes on cargo ships and tankers in the Red Sea.
The group exploited the chaos of the 2011 Arab Spring to oust the internationally recognised government from Sanaa in 2014, beginning the devastating Yemeni civil war.
Fearing the Iran-aligned group could seize control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and therefore threaten Riyadh’s ability to export oil, Saudi Arabia intervened a year later, supported by the US, UK, France and others.
A UN-brokered ceasefire followed in 2022 and since then, both sides have refrained from major escalatory actions. Iran has not directly intervened in Yemen, but the fighting is considered part of a wider Iran-Saudi proxy conflict.
It was during the Israeli war in Gaza, from 2023 to 2025, that the Houthis started attacking ships in the Red Sea in support of Iran-aligned Hamas. The UK and US hit Houthi targets in 2025 as part of a campaign to restore freedom of navigation.
Crucially, Trump last year struck a deal to end the US strikes on the Houthis in exchange for a halt to strikes on Red Sea shipping. Taking on the group now would likely expose US forces in the region to missile attacks from Yemen.
Clashes with Saudi Arabia restarted in July as both sides enforced new blockades on maritime traffic. The Houthis struck Saudi oil tankers accused of violating their blockade.
What are they doing now?
Despite years of conflict – and with some 14 per cent of Yemen’s population displaced – the Houthis last week oversaw an astonishing push east to the coast, granting them much greater control over traffic through the Red Sea.
The escalation has since expanded into a direct campaign against Saudi territory. Over the weekend, a barrage of Houthi missile and drone strikes hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 13 people — including a US citizen — and injuring more than 300.
Additional strikes targeting Saudi energy infrastructure and municipal facilities have forced temporary airport closures and heightened regional security alerts.
Edmund Fitton-Brown, a former UK ambassador to Yemen, told The Independent that after months of attacks at sea, the Houthis “think the moment has come to call the Saudi bluff”.
“They think the Saudis have lost the stomach for the fight. They think that they showed themselves to be weak and frightened in the face of the Iranians,” said Mr Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“And the Houthis think that this is the moment where they can effectively raise their demands and get the Saudis to concede even more advantageous terms than they were previously willing to do.”
With Iran controlling the strait on one side of the Arabian peninsula, and the allied Houthis controlling the other, the wider war has handed more regional influence in the region to Tehran, with Gulf countries now forced to accept they may have to engage with Iran and give up their faith in Washington as a guarantor of security.
The war presents the US with a dilemma, too: intervene and spend huge resources on a second front in the deeply unpopular war with Iran, or watch on and undermine the relationship with another ally in the region. Sources told CNN that the US has offered intelligence and targeting support to the Saudis in lieu of military support.
How are the Houthis breaching Saudi’s air defences?
While Saudi Arabia operates advanced air defence networks — including US-supplied Patriot and THAAD missile batteries — Houthi attacks continue to slip through.
This is because the Houthis rely on a combination of staggered salvoes and mixed arsenals to overwhelm radar capabilities. By launching slow-moving suicide drones first, followed by low-altitude cruise missiles and high-speed ballistic missiles only minutes later, the Houthis force defensive systems to engage multiple distinct threats arriving at the exact same moment.
Low-flying drones often bypass long-range radar designed primarily to track high-altitude targets. At the same time, the vast geographical footprint of the kingdom — covering major airports, military bases, and oil fields across millions of square kilometres — makes complete coverage nearly impossible.
The tactic also imposes a severe cost asymmetry on defenders. Firing multi-million-dollar interceptors to destroy cheap, assembled drones rapidly drains Saudi and allied missile stockpiles during sustained multi-wave attacks.
What has changed on the ground?
Houthi commanders announced a broad offensive targeting critical energy infrastructure and urban centres across southern and central Saudi Arabia as their ground forces pushed west.
The capture of key coastal hubs like al-Mokha and strategic points on Perim Island effectively divides the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Middle East analyst Fawaz Gerges described the seizure of key positions along the waterway as a structural shift in regional dynamics.
“It changes the balance of power and gives them far greater geopolitical and geoeconomic leverage over Saudi Arabia, the Gulf, the United States and global trade,” he said.
Concurrently, attacks attributed to regional proxy networks struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, severely impacting the primary overland bypass used to transport crude past the blocked Strait of Hormuz.
Sources told Reuters that rising economic losses and Washington's initial reluctance to launch direct strikes are convincing several Gulf leaderships that diplomatic outreach to Tehran may be necessary for self-preservation.
What happens next?
Mr Fitton-Brown said the region was calling for American leadership to recognise the connectedness between the fronts and intervene, where the Saudis have been unable to uphold maritime law.
“For the Americans to ignore the Red Sea, to ignore this threat to Saudi Arabia from the Houthis, is just completely self-defeating,” he said.
He said he would expect the US to remain “flaky” on the issue for now – but not back out entirely.
“They’re not going to fall on their sword because every so often these provocations will cross a threshold where they have no choice but to respond,” he said.
The challenge would be to bring together a “hybrid” coalition, including some military participants, but also countries willing to enforce sanctions and join a diplomatic coalition to force Iran to “back down”.
“It can be done, but it requires a level of diplomatic patience,” he said.
Lindsay Newman, associate fellow with Chatham House, said that one of the major open questions was the resilience of Iran’s proxy network across the region. While Hamas and Hezbollah have been degraded, the Houthi military “are proving more intractable” despite efforts to stop them.
Crucially, she said, this was not addressed by June’s interim agreement between the US and Iran. Washington had been pushing to raise the issue of Iran’s support for regional proxies before the war broke out in February.
“[The] developments make clear that a resolution on the proxy question must be integrated into any offramp for the wider regional conflict. Otherwise these groups can and likely will resupply and remain disruptive across the region.”

articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.
A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.
Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has said it will temporarily suspend flights to Riyadh and the north-eastern city of Dammam.
Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption".
King Khalid airport is expected to remain closed until Saturday.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said early on Tuesday that the Houthis had shot down what he described as a Saudi "reconnaissance drone".
Meanwhile, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed "two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait", in a statement shared on Tuesday.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
Meanwhile, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title: Houthis claim new attack on Riyadh airport, strike on Saudi air base
articles.summary: The Houthi group claimed Monday evening a fresh attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which it said it targeted with a ballistic missile and another drone attack o...
articles.full_text:
The Houthi group claimed Monday evening a fresh attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which it said it targeted with a ballistic missile and another drone attack on Khamis Mushait air base in southern Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement on X that the group had fired a ballistic missile at the airport, claiming the strike was "accurate."
Earlier, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced the "interception and destruction of a ballistic missile" launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh, without providing further details.
The coalition’s announcement coincided with Saudi Civil Defense declaring that the danger had passed in Riyadh, minutes after issuing an early warning over a potential danger.
In the same statement, Saree said the Iran-backed group had also carried out a drone attack on the Khamis Mushait air base, claiming a "direct hit."
There was no immediate Saudi comment on the claim concerning the air base.
Saree renewed the group’s warning to airlines, employees and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, claiming they were "unsafe," while excluding airports and airspace in Mecca and Medina.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of attacks on airports and civilian facilities in recent days.
Saudi Information Minister Salman Al-Dosari said Monday that the kingdom was prepared for various scenarios, regardless of their likelihood, stressing that life was continuing normally despite repeated Houthi attacks.
Speaking at a government press conference in Riyadh, according to the Saudi Press Agency, Al-Dosari said: "Life in the kingdom, praise be to God, continues normally."
"Increasing readiness does not mean anxiety; rather, it reflects the state's preparedness for various scenarios, whatever the likelihood of their occurrence," he added.
Despite the attacks, the World Petroleum Congress opened Sunday in Riyadh with broad international participation, although some executives have dropped out from the conference following the deadly attacks in recent days.
Saudi Arabia is hosting the event for the first time, with proceedings scheduled to conclude on Thursday.
Meanwhile, oil prices also rose on Monday as Houthis launched additional strikes, adding to worries about tight global supplies heading into the northern hemisphere winter.
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night following a series of Houthi attacks at the Riyadh airport in recent days that have killed at least 18 people.

articles.title: Houthis hit Riyadh airport again day after strike killed dozen
articles.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday night carried out a fresh strike on a passenger terminal at Riyadh's international airport, the Saudi-led coalition said, one day after a missile hi...
articles.full_text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday night carried out a fresh strike on a passenger terminal at Riyadh's international airport, the Saudi-led coalition said, one day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport – struck four times in the past five days – has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.
On Sunday night the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz – along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran's most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month.
The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels' strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels' use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon.
Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The ministry also claimed 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday's attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national.
Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety.
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they're pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 cease-fire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels' pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Futuristic Neom Stadium project put on hold - StadiumDB.com
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia: Futuristic Neom Stadium project put on hold  StadiumDB.com
articles.full_text:
The futuristic Neom Stadium, one of the most spectacular projects planned for the 2034 World Cup, has been put on hold indefinitely. Saudi Arabia still insists its tournament preparations are moving forward, but problems with Vision 2030 megaprojects raise questions over the final shape of the World Cup stadium network.
Neom Stadium was meant to be a stadium of the future
According to the documentation submitted as part of Saudi Arabia’s World Cup bid, the stadium was supposed to accommodate 46,000 spectators. Its extraordinary location, high above ground level, was intended to become one of the symbols of the tournament and the entire The Line project.
Neom was presented as one of the pillars of the Vision 2030 programme, which aims to diversify the economy and reduce the country’s dependence on oil exports. The development of sport, the hosting of major events and the construction of modern infrastructure were also intended to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s international image.
However, the scale of the undertaking proved enormous. According to data from the MEED Projects platform, the cost of building the stadium alone was estimated at around $2.5 billion. No completion date has currently been set for the project.
© Saudi Arabian Football Federation | The futuristic Neom Stadium was meant to be a symbol of the 2034 World Cup, but its construction has been postponed indefinitely.
Saudi Arabia changes its investment priorities
According to Reuters, which cited two sources familiar with the matter, construction of the stadium has been put on hold indefinitely. The possible suspension of work on Neom Stadium is part of a broader shift in Saudi Arabia’s approach to its megaprojects. In April, Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), confirmed that The Line was no longer a priority and did not have to be completed within the originally planned timeframe. However, he denied that any projects had been formally cancelled.
Reuters had previously also reported the suspension of work on the Mukaab, a huge cube-shaped skyscraper planned as part of the New Murabba development in Riyadh. The PIF is gradually shifting its focus away from expensive projects with distant returns towards ventures that can deliver financial benefits sooner.
Pressure on the budget is increasing due to difficult conditions in the oil market, disruptions to the transportation of raw materials and the consequences of the armed conflict in the region. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Finance has also forecast a larger budget deficit than previously expected.
© Saudi Arabian Football Federation | Saudi Arabia is still preparing 15 stadiums for the 2034 World Cup, although the future of the venue in The Line remains uncertain.
The 2034 World Cup remains a strategic objective
The problems surrounding Neom Stadium do not mean that Saudi Arabia is abandoning its plans to host the World Cup. The tournament remains one of the country’s most important undertakings, with preparations including the construction and modernisation of 15 stadiums in five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities.
According to MEED Projects, the combined value of stadium projects and related infrastructure is expected to reach around $22.7 billion. Saudi authorities maintain that preparations for the tournament are progressing, although they have not directly answered questions about the future of Neom Stadium.
Uncertainty surrounding Neom Stadium raises questions about the final shape of the World Cup infrastructure. Experts quoted by Deutsche Welle suggest that Saudi Arabia could rely more heavily on its two largest urban centres – Riyadh and Jeddah. Under such a scenario, the importance of some venues closer to the eastern coast could be reassessed in light of the geopolitical situation.
However, there is no confirmation that the number of stadiums selected to host the World Cup will be reduced. Neither FIFA, Saudi sports authorities nor the body responsible for organising the tournament has issued an official statement on the matter in response to questions from Deutsche Welle.
The 2022 World Cup in Qatar is often cited as a point of comparison in this debate. Twelve stadiums were initially planned, but the tournament was ultimately played across eight venues. This does not mean, however, that Saudi Arabia will necessarily follow the same path.

articles.title: Bangladesh seeks stronger energy ties with Saudi Arabia, Qatar - The Financial Express
articles.summary: Bangladesh seeks stronger energy ties with Saudi Arabia, Qatar  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh has sought stronger energy cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Qatar while exploring foreign investment opportunities in its renewable energy sector during a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the 17th International Energy Forum held in Riyadh.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit held separate meetings with Saudi Assistant Minister of Energy for Electricity Nasser bin Hadi Al-Qahtani, Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs and Qatar Energy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, and ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan, according to a message received in Dhaka on Monday.
The discussions focused on strengthening Bangladesh's energy security, securing long-term liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, expanding bilateral cooperation and attracting foreign investment in renewable energy.
During his meeting with Saudi Assistant Minister Nasser Al-Qahtani, Amit expressed condolences over the deaths caused by a Houthi rebel attack at Riyadh International Airport and condemned the attack.
He reaffirmed the solidarity of the government and people of Bangladesh with Saudi Arabia and briefed the Saudi official on the condolence message sent by Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the Saudi crown prince and prime minister.
The Bangladesh state minister also sought Saudi Arabia's assistance in repatriating the bodies of two Bangladeshi nationals killed in the attack and ensuring medical treatment for those injured.
On energy cooperation, Amit sought Saudi support to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. In response, the Saudi official described Bangladesh as a brotherly country that holds special importance for the Saudi government and expressed optimism about further expanding ongoing cooperation in energy security and other development initiatives.
The two sides stressed exchanging delegations and establishing a framework for understanding to discuss areas of Saudi support for Bangladesh's efforts to achieve its energy targets by 2030.
The discussions also covered long-term energy cooperation, the development of floating LNG terminals, and offshore and onshore gas exploration.
In his meeting with Qatar's State Minister for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Amit discussed Bangladesh's growing demand for natural gas, its existing LNG import arrangements and the possibility of signing new long-term supply agreements.
The two sides also explored LNG supplies from Qatar Energy's international portfolio and the diversification of supply sources and routes to strengthen Bangladesh's energy security. Both ministers stressed the need for continuing commercial and technical discussions between the relevant organisations.
In a third meeting, ACWA Power CEO Dr Samir J Serhan discussed investment opportunities in Bangladesh's renewable energy sector with the state minister. ACWA Power expressed interest in investing in the country's renewable energy sector.
Officials from the Bangladesh delegation and the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh were present at the meetings.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia - DW.com
articles.summary: Germany's Wadephul calls new EU sanctions 'unprecedented' blow to Russia  DW.comEU sanctions nearly 1,600 Russian people and firms linked to drone and missile parts  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosEurope pushes tougher line on Russia in growing split with Trump  POLITICO.euRussia’s war of aggression against Ukraine: EU agrees largest-ever package of listings targeting almost 1600 individuals and entities in Russia’s military-industrial complex ...
articles.full_text:
German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
Who do the sanctions target?
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.
"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
What is the latest development in the war?
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.
US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

articles.title: Bunkers, handpicked guards: How Saudi Prince MBS moves between palaces amid Houthi threat - The Times of India
articles.summary: Bunkers, handpicked guards: How Saudi Prince MBS moves between palaces amid Houthi threat  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers as the kingdom faces renewed Houthi attacks amid the wider conflict linked to the Iran war, as reported by the Wall Street Journal.
The crown prince’s last public appearance was on Tuesday, when he donated blood as part of a national donation drive.
The 41-year-old crown prince is being protected by a handpicked security team, officials familiar with his movements said, as reported by Wall Street Journal.
Saudi Arabia is struggling to shield key infrastructure and economic assets from further Houthi aattacks.
At least one Houthi missile struck Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, killing at least 12 people and injuring hundreds, many of them seriously. It was the deadliest attack on the United States or its Gulf allies in conflicts linked to the Iran war.
The Houthis have struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh at least four times.
Prince Mohammed brought Saudi Arabia into Yemen’s civil war in 2015, backing the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. The Saudi-led intervention involved devastating airstrikes that intensified the conflict and fuelled the Houthis’ campaign against the kingdom, including attacks on oil facilities and cities such as Riyadh.
The two sides fought to a stalemate before agreeing to a ceasefire in 2022.
The latest outbreak of violence comes as Prince Mohammed seeks to contain the confrontation with Iran. Attacks launched by Tehran early in the war exposed the vulnerability of energy facilities and economic assets, including airports, across the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia is also struggling to provide air defence coverage across its vast territory. The kingdom has been shifting air defence batteries to protect palaces and energy infrastructure, people familiar with its deliberations said.
Saudi Arabia is also seeking a more direct US role in countering Houthi attacks. Washington has provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning support for a Saudi-led offensive but has so far refrained from launching strikes against the rebels.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he was considering military action against the Houthis following the deadly attack on Riyadh’s international airport.
However, US intervention could widen the conflict and threaten a critical global shipping route. The Houthis could attempt to disrupt traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden near Yemen.
Such a disruption could further restrict global oil supplies, already affected by Iran’s efforts to choke off the Strait of Hormuz. Before the US-Iran war began, about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strategic waterway.
The Houthis seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb last month. The Saudi-led coalition, which backs forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to retake those areas.

articles.title: Pakistan confirms it has troops in Saudi as conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalates - Egypt Independent
articles.summary: Pakistan confirms it has troops in Saudi as conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalates  Egypt Independent
articles.full_text:
“The forces of Pakistan are already there. That I can share with you,” Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told CNN in an exclusive interview on Wednesday, without specifying how many or their capabilities, saying those details were classified.
The confirmation from Chaudhry, the chief of the Pakistani military’s media wing, came just days after the two nations and Turkey agreed to the rapid deployment of the forces, as part of a newly minted mutual defense treaty.
Over the past two days, the Houthis have killed three people in attacks on Saudi’s Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border, and King Khalid International Airport, in the capital Riyadh, Saudi officials said.
The attacks underscore how the conflict is increasingly affecting Saudi territory as Riyadh deepens its support for the Yemeni government’s military campaign.
The targeting of the airports prompted an updated security alert from the US Mission in Saudi Arabia, warning American citizens the conflict “has the potential to escalate.”
The Iran-backed Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015.
The conflict flared up in July, shortly after the US-Iran ceasefire unravelled, with Houthi missile attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in an expansion of the Middle East war. Riyadh has responded with airstrikes in support of Yemeni government forces.
In recent days, Yemeni government forces have claimed advances near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, which the Houthis claimed effective control of last month. The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Pakistan’s troops in Saudi
The escalation has coincided with Saudi moves to strengthen defense cooperation with regional military heavyweights Turkey, a NATO member, and nuclear-armed Pakistan The trio recently signed a pact with NATO-style collective defense provisions, often referred to as the Mecca Alliance.
The deployment of Pakistani forces had “not come out of a vacuum” Chaudhry, Director General of the Inter-Services Public Relations, told CNN. Pakistan has had a military presence in Saudi Arabia for decades, he said.
Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi’s security was “absolute,” Chaudhry said. He described the alliance as a mechanism for collective defense under which an attack on one member would be considered an attack on all.
But he would not be drawn on whether Pakistani troops would be involved in any operations across the border in Yemen. “Whenever there is a military conflict, no participating country starts disclosing how and where it is going to employ its forces,” he said, adding the any involvement would be “defensive in nature.”
“The objective of this alliance is not to start labelling enemies, enemies, enemies, friends, friends, friends. The objective is the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia… That will be done,” said Chaudhry.
In a joint statement following an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the three countries said they would move immediately to implement collective defense commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Chaudhry said the collective security agreement would also act as a deterrent.
“Anyone having some funny ideas against another will hopefully think twice, thrice, or multiple times before doing that. That stops something terrible from happening.”
Coming to Saudi’s defense is nevertheless complex calculation for Pakistan, which has played a key role in mediating between Iran – its neighbor and backer of the Houthis – and the US, since the US and Israel launched their war with Iran.
In 2015, Pakistan’s parliament voted against sending troops to assist Saudi Arabia in an earlier round of fighting against the Houthis in Yemen.
Chaudhry said Pakistan was still pushing for a deal to end the US-Iran war.
“We have done, are doing, and will continue to do whatever is possible and necessary so that the differences and the gaps narrow down and there is a negotiated, peaceful outcome. We want this conflict not to expand.”
Houthi airport attacks
The Houthi-controlled armed forces said they fired a ballistic missile towards Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport on Wednesday, in an attack Saudi authorities say killed a Sudanese resident and wounded eight others.
Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, later said Saudi forces had destroyed the ballistic missile launcher used in the Riyadh attack, adding that preparations were underway for “another imminent attack.”
The attack on the Abha International Airport on Tuesday killed two female residents, one Moroccan and one Algerian national, and wounded 28 others, said Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation. The Houthi claimed responsibility for both attacks.
This week, Houthi fighters also used ballistic missiles to target the international airport in Aden – which serves as the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, and an important transit hub for areas outside of Houthi control.
The missiles landed near the airport’s runway shortly before a Yemenia Airways flight from Cairo had been due to land, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi’s Jeddah, Yemen’s Transport ministry said on Wednesday.
The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press ahead with Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at rolling back recent Houthi gains.
Last month, the Houthis seized effective control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway for the global oil trade – after claiming key Yemeni positions along the Red Sea coastline. But in recent days Yemeni forces have claimed to have retaken some of those positions.
With civilian infrastructure now coming under renewed attack, the hostilities are showing signs of expanding beyond the battlefield in Yemen and posing a growing challenge to Saudi security and transportation networks.

articles.title: Watch: Why is it so hard to fight the Houthis? - BBC
articles.summary: Watch: Why is it so hard to fight the Houthis?  BBC
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed to respond to the attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
It comes after the Houthis fired missiles in strikes across Riyadh, killing at least 14 and injured more than 300 in two strikes on the city's airport. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The BBC's security correspondent Frank Gardner explains how Houthis' precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it difficult for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand.

articles.title: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want? - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
A strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded 309, in the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade. Another strike on the airport on Sunday killed one more person.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen's Houthis and called the attack a war crime.
In a statement on Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted the airport "in three stages" since Friday evening, closing it completely, and warned that Saudi airports were "unsafe", except those serving Mecca and Medina.
The attack capped a summer of escalation. A UN-backed truce that had largely frozen Yemen's war since 2022 broke down in July after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport, and the Houthis then declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom.
In September, the Sanaa-based group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and pushed towards the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Saudi-backed government forces launched a counter-offensive in early October, and the UN special envoy has warned that Yemen has returned to full-scale war.
Heavy clashes are continuing around the strategically important city of Taiz, which sits above the Red Sea coast. The renewed fighting has displaced 130,000 people.
Who are the Houthis?
Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi.
It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands.
The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement.
Houthi fighters captured Sanaa in September 2014, and in March 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition into Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government, which has mostly governed from Riyadh and the southern Yemeni city of Aden.
By the time of the 2022 truce, the Houthis held about 30 percent of Yemen's territory but around 80 percent of its population.
What do they want?
At home, the Houthis have sought greater autonomy for the north and, increasingly, recognition as Yemen's governing authority.
They have demanded an end to what they describe as a Saudi land, air and naval siege of Yemen, a characterisation Riyadh rejects.
In his statement on Sunday, Saree said the group would keep escalating attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia under what he called an equation of "siege for siege, escalation for escalation", until the "aggression" stopped and the siege on Yemen was lifted.
Their ambitions, however, extend beyond Yemen.
The movement's frames its politics in opposition to US and Israeli power in the region.
Since 2023, the group has attacked more than 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying it was acting in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel's genocide in Gaza. The strikes were temporarily halted in May 2025 in a ceasefire deal with Washington, brokered by Oman.
In March, it began firing missiles at Israel in support of Tehran after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.
How close are they to Iran?
Iran counts Ansar Allah as part of its "Axis of Resistance" alongside Hezbollah and Hamas, and has courted the group since at least the late 2000s. Much of the Houthi arsenal has been designed or supplied by Tehran.
The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy.
After the Riyadh strikes, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that Tehran was "deeply concerned" by the escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and offered to help facilitate dialogue between the two sides.
How strong are they militarily?
The Houthi fighting force grew from an estimated 30,000 in 2015 to around 350,000 by 2024, although counts vary.
The group has no conventional navy and little air power, but it fields drones, explosive-laden drone boats and medium-range ballistic missiles that have reached targets about 2,000km away in Israel.
Why does the Bab al-Mandab matter?
The strait links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is the southern approach to the Suez Canal.
Its importance has grown since the war on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil prices and leaving the Red Sea as a key alternative route for Saudi exports.

Good morning, ladies and gents. We have a somber start to the week: two Saudi airports were hit again yesterday. The Houthis have claimed four attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities in 24 hours. Saudi authorities confirmed the strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid and Dammam’s King Fahd airports. King Khalid is shut after Saturday’s missile strike killed 13 people.
Meanwhile, Qatar’s first North Field East LNG train is ready to run next month, a dozen empty carriers are waiting near Qatar to load, and Aramco is in talks to make loading outside Hormuz a standard part of its 2027 crude contracts.
Also in today’s issue: Sharjah is pitching Khorfakkan to Indian investors as a way around Hormuz, and Agility Global has raised EUR 500 mn from international lenders.
The Gulf’s sovereign funds and largest companies are committing billions to AI infrastructure at home and to AI companies in the US and beyond. EnterpriseAM AI + Innovation reports on where that capital goes, who controls it and what it is actually buying.
Every Tuesday and Thursday, we also cover the startups and established firms across MENA putting AI to work, and how it is changing jobs, education and the way business runs.
It’s sharp, analytical and skeptical journalism that ignores hype and is laser-focused on informing our readers, not pleasing our sources.
Sign up here to be among the first to get it straight to your inbox.
Sharjah wants India’s next Gulf base
With Hormuz routes crippled and Jebel Ali bottlenecks mounting, Sharjah is playing its geopolitical trump card. The emirate is leveraging a USD 2 bn expansion at Khorfakkan Commercial Terminal to target USD 3 bn in Indian FDI across 2026 and 2027, Economic Times reports. It is the UAE's only fully commercial deep-water port sitting safely outside the Strait of the Gulf of Oman.
The pitch is regional: Companies can use Sharjah as a base to reach Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Iraq, and wider Gulf markets, while staying connected to east-west maritime routes. The Sharjah FDI Office expects about USD 1.5 bn this year and another USD 1.5 bn next year — a roughly 15% surge from the previous year. Manufacturers and logistics majors are rapidly securing industrial acreage around Khorfakkan to establish export hubs serving Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Iraq without braving maritime chokepoints.
Khorfakkan opens up: The emirate is seeing rising enquiries from manufacturing, logistics, and transportation companies, and strong demand for industrial land near the port, said Mohamed Juma Al Musharrkh, CEO of Invest in Sharjah.
IN CONTEXT- Port operator Gulftainer is actively scaling Khorfakkan’s container capacity from 3.5 mn to 5 mn TEUs, eyeing a long-term 10 mn TEU target.
Seasonal slowdown
The Egyptian government has cut its planned October LNG purchases by 40% to 12 cargoes, down from 20, as cooler weather eases power demand, Asharq Business reports, citing an unnamed government official. Volumes could still change depending on domestic demand and global prices, the official added.
Each cargo still costs close to USD 100 mn: With LNG at around USD 28 per mmBtu, shipping, ins., and financing come on top of that, the official said. That means the import bill won’t necessarily fall in step with volumes. The government has earmarked USD 10.7 bn for natural gas imports this fiscal year.
We’ve seen this pattern before: Last October, the government cut its planned October LNG arrivals to six cargoes from 19 as domestic consumption eased. The seasonal slowdown had already left tankers queuing to unload in late September. But the relief proved temporary, and by November we were back on the market, seeking additional cargoes to fill the supply gap.
The gas crunch gave Egypt every reason to speed up its energy transition, and the question now is who builds it and who pays for it.
Power Trip, our four-part signature series, turns this week to the transition and the private developers now building much of Egypt’s new power.
Issue II looks at how the deals behind these projects work, who is lending to them, and why the country is building a nuclear plant at El Dabaa alongside its solar and wind farms. We also look at whether the regional crisis has finally pushed industry toward renewables, and at the factories Egypt is counting on to build its own panels, batteries, and turbines.
