Market watch
Oil prices fell on expectations of higher Russian supply after a reported halt in attacks on energy facilities, Reuters reports. Brent crude futures slipped USD 1.54 to USD 103.18 / bbl by 01.54 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) declined USD 1.54 to USD 90.31 / bbl.
The Baltic Index extends its slide: The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk index — which tracks rates for the capesize, panamax, and supramax vessel segments — fell 2.2% to 3,002 points on Friday. The capesize index dropped 4% to 4,638 points, while the panamax edged up 0.1% to 2,366 points. The smaller supramax gained 0.3% to 1,795 points.
The Drewry World Container Index fell 2% to USD 4,351 per 40-ft container last week, according to the latest index readings. Transpacific rates slipped, with Shanghai-Los Angeles down 3% and Shanghai-New York down 2%, while Shanghai-Rotterdam fell 2% and Shanghai-Genoa held flat. China’s Golden Week closures are weighing on cargo flows, and rising Suez Canal transits are adding effective capacity to Asia-Europe routes. Drewry expects volatility to continue as demand, capacity, and geopolitical risks move rates.

articles.title: Unexploded ordnance blast kills 1 near Israel-Lebanon border
articles.summary: An unexploded ordnance blast near Israel's northern border with Lebanon killed at least one hiker and injured 19 others Monday, Israeli media reported. The daily Yedioth Ahronoth r...
articles.full_text:
An unexploded ordnance blast near Israel's northern border with Lebanon killed at least one hiker and injured 19 others Monday, Israeli media reported.
The daily Yedioth Ahronoth reported that one of the hikers injured in the blast during an annual school trip had died, citing the MDA emergency service.
Earlier, the agency said one person was in critical condition and two others were seriously injured.
The blast occurred in the Ramim Ridge area along the Lebanon border and involved an organized hiking group from a middle school, according to newspaper.
"Unfortunately there is unexploded ordnance, apparently someone accidentally touched an explosive device," the father of one of the injured was quoted as saying.
The Times of Israel news portal earlier said the blast was believed to have been caused by "unexploded ordnance," though authorities were still investigating the exact cause.

articles.title: Iran maintains indirect comms as it weighs US' Hormuz plan reply
articles.summary: Iran continues to review a U.S. response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and will reply through intermediaries once the review is complete, Foreign Ministry spokespe...
articles.full_text:
Iran continues to review a U.S. response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and will reply through intermediaries once the review is complete, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday.
Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
"The exchange of messages between Iran and the U.S. through mediators continues," Baghaei said.
"We are reviewing the Americans’ proposals for negotiations. Iran’s preconditions must be observed for any negotiations," he added.
After a June interim cease-fire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a U.S. response.
However, the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear program from the outset.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) and restoring security in the waterway.
Baqhaei added that Russia also continues to play a "constructive" role regarding Iran’s nuclear file, pointing to Moscow’s involvement in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
He said Iranian and Russian relations are based on mutual trust and that Tehran welcomes supportive efforts by friendly countries, but stressed that, "technically and precisely," mediation between Iran and the U.S. remains in the hands of countries such as Pakistan and Qatar.
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Baqhaei said developments there were a direct consequence of U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran and rejected suggestions that Tehran’s actions were intended to create negotiating leverage.
"What we have seen in the Strait of Hormuz since Feb. 28 was the direct result of the U.S. and the Israeli regime's attack on Iran," he said.
"With the current U.S. approach, security will not return," he added.
Baqhaei rejected U.S. assertions that Iran had lost its leverage, saying such claims did not correspond with realities on the ground.
"They can say Iran has lost its leverage, but we are doing our work," he said, arguing that energy markets were not responding to Washington’s assertions.
Baqhaei also said that Iran was "deeply concerned" by escalating attacks between Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh's airport.
"We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula," he said, adding that Tehran was ready "to help facilitate dialogue between the parties."
A Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
"We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries," Baqhaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation "through dialogue and engagement."
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed "Axis of Resistance," a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

articles.title: Truce-violating Israel kills 5 Palestinians in Gaza in 24 hours
articles.summary: An Israeli strike killed at least two people in southern Gaza Monday, health officials said, day after killing three more across the Palestinian enclave. Two casualties were report...
articles.full_text:
An Israeli strike killed at least two people in southern Gaza Monday, health officials said, day after killing three more across the Palestinian enclave.
Two casualties were reported when an Israeli drone hit a group of Palestinians northwest of Rafah, the sources said, as Israel continues to violate a cease-fire in effect since last October.
The drone fired at least one missile at the group near Muawiya Mosque in the al-Mawasi area northwest of the city, according to witnesses.
Separately, Israeli artillery fired shells toward areas northeast of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, locals said.
Israeli naval forces also opened fire and launched shells toward the Gaza City coast in the north, with no injuries reported, they added.
Earlier Sunday, three Palestinians were killed and several others injured Sunday in an Israeli drone strike on a tent in southern Gaza.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said the bodies of three Palestinians and several wounded people were brought to the facility after the strike near the hospital in the southern al-Buraq area of central Khan Younis.
Witnesses told Anadolu Agency (AA) that an Israeli drone fired at least one missile at the tent, which was being used as a mobile phone charging point.
Also Sunday, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital said Jihad Iyad al-Ghandour, 6, died of serious wounds sustained Saturday when Israeli soldiers opened fire in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza.
Separately, Israeli forces expanded the area under their control in eastern Gaza City early Sunday, injuring two Palestinians, including a pregnant woman and forcing dozens of families to flee their homes, according to local Palestinian sources.
The sources told AA that Israeli military vehicles advanced tens of meters beyond their existing positions in the Shujaiya neighborhood overnight from Saturday into Sunday, under cover of heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.
They said the troops were accompanied by armed Palestinian militias cooperating with and supported by the Israeli army, while quadcopter drones provided cover.
Israeli forces fired heavily toward the area stretching from the vegetable market in the east to the Shujaiya intersection on Salah al-Din Street in the west, the sources added.
For about a week, eastern areas of Gaza, particularly the eastern parts of the Tuffah and Shujaiya neighborhoods, have witnessed nighttime demolitions, gunfire, heavy artillery shelling and military vehicle movements near the "yellow line," according to the sources.
The line separates areas occupied by Israeli forces in the east from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain in the west.
Israeli cease-fire violations have killed 1,488 Palestinians and injured 5,281 as of Sunday, according to the latest figures from Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since the war began in October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured, while around 90% of Gaza's infrastructure has been destroyed, according to the ministry.

articles.title: The bourgeois war of annihilation against Israel - Spiked
articles.summary: The bourgeois war of annihilation against Israel  SpikedThree years of war, 100,000 targets struck: IDF releases new conflict data  Breaking DefenseA Small Portland Gathering Speaks of Gazan Suffering on Oct. 7 Anniversary  Willamette WeekAnalysis • In the Jewish Diaspora, it's still October 8  HaaretzThree years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
The third anniversary of 7 October made it crystal clear: the Western left and Hamas both want to destroy the Jewish nation.
If Zohran Mamdani had a functioning moral compass, Wednesday would have been the wake-up call of this life. There he was in Union Square being heckled by a feral mob. Their faces hardened into snarls of hatred, they barked ‘Shame on you!’ at the New York mayor. And they were radical leftists, the kind of people who normally gush over Mamdani’s reactionary Third Worldist guff. What sin had he committed to irk his erstwhile fawners? He commemorated Jewish suffering.
That was it. Nothing more, nothing less. He attended an Israelis for Peace vigil on the third anniversary of the 7 October pogrom to pay tribute to the men, women and children slaughtered by Hamas. For that he was damned as a stooge of a genocidal regime. ‘Zohran you can’t hide / We charge you with genocide!’, howled the mob. Some chased him, screaming: ‘Traitor!’ To a Jew hater, sympathy for Jews is high treason.
There’s no denying it now: the Hamasniks of the Islamo-left enjoy Jewish suffering. They crave it. Indeed, some of Mamdani’s scolds waved the Hamas flag and hollered, ‘We support Hamas’. They were mad at the mayor because he had the temerity to look sad about the slaughter of Jews. To these keffiyeh Nazis, when Hamas kills Jews it’s ‘resistance’, and when Jews fight back it’s ‘genocide’. They call themselves anti-fascists yet hail from the same violent, vomitous gutter as the mobs of Kristallnacht.
And yet, even the mockery of Jews at a commemoration for dead Jews is unlikely to wake Mamdani to the horrors of the Gaza cult. Indeed, that mob in Union Square was a monster of his own making. He has made anti-Israel hate respectable in New York City. He refuses to call Hamas terrorists. His own statement on the third anniversary of 7 October spent a few poxy lines condemning Hamas’s ‘crimes’ before raging at length against Israel’s ‘devastating, ongoing genocide’. He had no right to look shook when the keffiyeh fash turned a commemoration of the slaughter of Jews into a Two Minutes Hate against the Jewish nation – he did it first.
For the rest of us, though, it’s time to get real. That crowds feel confident to gloat over the mass murder of Jews is the clearest sign you could ask that a spiritual sickness ails the West. And it’s not just NYC. Across the West last Wednesday, there were orgies of ecstasy over the butchery carried out by Hamas three years ago. In Amsterdam a mob marched with a banner saying ‘We support Hamas’. They screamed ‘Long live 7 October’. In Edinburgh, they marched behind a banner saying ‘Glory to our martyrs’. The martyrs they were referring to were the Islamofascists who invaded Israel to rape and annihilate Jews.
In London, keffiyeh-adorned lowlifes gathered on 7 October to fume against the Jewish nation. Some made an inverted triangle with their fingers – a sly expression of support for the murderous violence of Hamas. In Italy, a mob celebrated 7 October as ‘one of the most significant [acts] of Palestinian Resistance’. Across the West there were scores of anti-Israel gatherings on the day Israelis mourned the rape and destruction of more than a thousand of their citizens. There’s an all-out effort to redefine the day that Hamas unleashed genocidal violence on the Jews of the Holy Land as the day ‘Israel’s genocide’ started. The old Nazis stole Jews’ property – the new ones steal their days of commemoration.
Meanwhile, the Green Party of England and Wales voted in favour of the annihilation of the Jewish homeland. They are morally as one with Hamas, which is likewise fuelled by a genocidal urge to scrub Israel from the face of the Earth. The Green Party member who put forward this racist proposal to erase the Jews’ homeland has been exposed as a one-time ‘good friend’ of the al-Qaeda freak who plotted to make a rucksack bomb full of shrapnel dipped in rat poison and then blow himself up at Heathrow Airport with the aim of massacring passengers from Israel. Can we talk about this? The fact that a mainstream party in the UK is taking its moral cues from a member who was mates with an Islamist terrorist who dreamt of murdering Jews? The fact that the ‘anti-fascist’ left is lining up with a party that wants to destroy Israel, and which has members who called Jews cockroaches, and whose deputy leader celebrated the Jew-murder of 7 October with cackles of ‘Allahu Akbar’?
At least they can deny it no longer – their aim is not to end the war in Gaza but to end Israel. Their dream is not peace but annihilation. If the keffiyeh classes got their way, and Israel was dismantled, the consequence would be an extermination of Jews that would make 7 October look like a tea party. To Israel’s south is an army of anti-Semites (Hamas) that openly says it wants to cut off the heads of Jews. To its north is an Islamofascist outfit (Hezbollah) that calls Jews ‘apes and pigs’ and says they should fuck off ‘back to Germany, or wherever they came from’. And to its east is the Islamic Republic, a nation that entirely defines itself by its cosmic hostility to Jewish nationhood. To agitate for the dismantling of Israel in such circumstances is to agitate for the mass expulsion and the mass murder of Jews. Own it.
The longed-for erasure of Israel is justified through the erasure of Jewish history. Owen Jones spent last week arguing that Israel was ‘carved out of a land that was 90 per cent Arab Muslim and Christian’. He’s referring to 1917, the year of the Balfour Declaration. To single out that year without mentioning what preceded it or what followed it is one of the most sinister acts of Orwellian obfuscation I have ever seen from a mainstream journalist.
The reason Jews made up just 10 per cent of the Holy Land in the 1910s is because for centuries they had been violently expelled and violently converted by everyone from the Romans to the Arabs to the Ottomans. And to fail to mention the Fifth Aliyah of 1929 to 1939, when hundreds of thousands of Jews returned to Israel, is criminal. These were not ‘invading Zionists’ but Jews fleeing their ghettoisation, enslavement and burning to death by Nazis. Does Jones think they should have stayed in Europe? The depiction of Israel as a product of ‘Zionist invasion’ is the great lie of our times. In truth, Israel is a wholly anti-colonial enterprise born from the stirring refusal of Jews to be world-scattered targets for Nazi scum and peasant pogromists.
Last week, the mask – or the keffiyeh – truly slipped. Some of us have known since 8 October 2023, and earlier, that the ‘pro-Palestine’ movement is a regressive, bigoted crusade devoted less to the liberation of Palestinians than to the annihilation of Israel. That this is less about making a homeland for the Palestinians and more about dancing on the ashes of the homeland of the Jews. Surely now others can see it too? Anti-Semitism is always a catalyst for civilisational collapse, said Hannah Arendt, as it opens the doors to totalitarian movements. So it is today. Everyone who values reason, truth, liberty and basic human decency should stand with their every fibre against the bourgeois war of annihilation against the Jewish State.

articles.title: Drone Strike Targets Oil Tanker off Oman - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Drone Strike Targets Oil Tanker off Oman  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
An oil tanker came under a drone attack near the Port of Sohar in northern Oman, leaving two Indian sailors missing, while Iran claimed that the United States had accepted some of Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, highlighting parallel security and diplomatic tensions across the region.
India’s Shipping Minister, Sarbananda Sonowal, said the MT Petro Dolphin, carrying 11 Indian sailors, was attacked by a drone on Sunday while operating in an area under the jurisdiction of Sohar port.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had reclassified an incident near an anchorage off Sohar as an attack after confirming that an oil tanker had been struck by an unmanned aerial vehicle.
Local authorities were assisting with the evacuation of the crew, the agency said, adding that the extent of the damage and the potential environmental impact remained unclear. Two Indian sailors were reported missing following the incident.
The attack adds to concerns over maritime security in waters near the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic shipping corridor for global energy supplies.
Iran Says Washington Accepted Some Conditions
Separately, Iran said the United States had accepted some of its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, although Tehran described Washington’s response as insufficient and said several issues remained unresolved.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, was quoted by Iranian media on Sunday as saying that the US response to Tehran’s seven conditions was inadequate.
Iran had presented a proposal during the United Nations General Assembly offering to restore normal maritime traffic through the strait within seven days, provided its conditions were met. Washington subsequently responded through Qatari intermediaries, according to the report.
“We presented seven conditions to the Americans and made it clear that the Strait of Hormuz would not be opened to them, and no negotiations would take place until these conditions were fulfilled,” Rezaei said, according to Iranian media.
He added that Washington had accepted some of the conditions, while others remained unclear to Tehran.
The White House had not responded to a request for comment at the time of the report.
Diplomatic Efforts to Reopen the Strait
Tehran said in late September that it had received a US response to its latest proposals aimed at reviving a ceasefire that had collapsed. The development came days after US President Donald Trump said he had rejected the proposal.
Qatar and other intermediaries have continued to relay messages between Washington and Tehran as diplomatic efforts seek to end the conflict and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, which began in late February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, the strait handled roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making its disruption a major concern for international energy markets.
Maritime Security and Energy Risks
The tanker attack near Oman and the continuing dispute over the Strait of Hormuz underscore the security challenges facing commercial shipping in the region.
Any prolonged disruption to maritime traffic through the strait could have significant implications for energy transportation and global supply chains. However, the full consequences of the latest tanker incident remain uncertain, with damage assessments and the environmental impact yet to be established.
For now, the two developments point to a volatile regional situation in which maritime security incidents and diplomatic negotiations are unfolding simultaneously, while the prospects for restoring normal shipping through one of the world's most important energy corridors remain unresolved.

articles.full_text:
Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand Sunday in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country's longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance, with national elections just weeks away.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, was on high alert after a deadly attack on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, allegedly by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.
Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu's corruption case
Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand Sunday in Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial.
Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister.
Netanyahu was seated in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022.
“The truth comes to light,” Netanyahu said before entering the courtroom.
Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing.
The latest proceedings come weeks before national elections.
Saudi on high-alert after deadly attack, Houthi warn of new strikes
Saudi Arabia kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online on Sunday after a deadly strike by Yemen’s Houthi rebels the day before.
The rebels threatened new airstrikes across the kingdom after a missile attack on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 on Saturday. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for that, but claimed two previous deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport earlier in the week.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously.”
The airport strike marked a major escalation in the war between the Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom, and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.
U.S. President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to join Saudi strikes against the rebels, a scenario that could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through a crucial waterway and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.
Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue amid ceasefire
Residents in central Gaza returned home Sunday morning to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the buildings the day before.
Bassam Abed said that at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble. He said families were not given enough time to flee before the military struck their buildings.
“Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said.
The Israeli military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including three weapons storage facilities, a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to carry out attacks on Israeli soldiers.
The strikes fell one year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, but Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes.
Trump officially lifts ban on direct flight to Lebanon
The White House has officially lifted a decades-old ban on direct flight between the U.S. and Lebanon, following through on a commitment President Donald Trump made in July.
U.S. carriers may be reticent to begin offering flight to Lebanon soon, however, as the war with Iran continues to disrupts air traffic in the region and questions over Hezbollah’s influence in parts of the country persist. Direct flights between the two countries were suspended in 1985 by the Reagan administration after the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.
The Lebanese embassy in Washington said on social media that it welcomed the move as “a major step toward resuming direct flights.”
The U.S. embassy in Beirut said the change would make it easier for family members to visit one another and for American businesses to invest in Lebanon. “We look forward to working with our Lebanese partners to turn this opportunity into a reality,” the statement added.

articles.title: Abramovich’s close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest - BBC
articles.summary: Abramovich’s close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest  BBCDeloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds  BBCRoman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest  The GuardianAbramovich aides accused of hiding mansions and jets to avoid tax  The TelegraphAbramovich’s inner circle presented high court with sham documents and misleading testimony...
articles.full_text:
One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest.
Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won.
Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors.
The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture.
Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him".
Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court".
The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky.
Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields.
Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously.
Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge.
Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London.
At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about £1bn.
But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares.
Abramovich won the case on a number of fronts, including that Yugraneft's case had been an abuse of process.
However, Panorama has uncovered new evidence suggesting the court was misled, in a joint investigation with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.
The evidence is contained in a leak of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. It raises serious questions about the integrity of some of the oligarch's professional advisers.
We have already found that the world's biggest accountancy firm, Deloitte, helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.
In the High Court, lawyers for Yugraneft argued the case should be heard in London, and that Tenenbaum, who was based there at the time, must have been aware of the dilution of Yugraneft's interest.
But Tenenbaum denied this and told the court "he only became aware of Sibneft-Yugra in Spring 2004".
He also testified he had "searched" his "files, emails and documents from 2002 to 2004" and had in his "possession no records or documents or other communications that relate to Sibneft-Yugra".
But the leaked documents suggest he misled the court.
They show that in October 2003, months before Tenenbaum said he first became aware of Sibneft-Yugra, he had authorised Abramovich's purchase of shares in the joint venture.
Two months later, Tenenbaum authorised another financial deal related to Sibneft-Yugra.
Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, told Panorama that it would be "very serious" if Tenenbaum's 2008 evidence was false and that it could "range from being perjury, to an attempt to pervert the course of justice, to being a contempt of the court".
Tenenbaum's lawyers told us "he gave his evidence honestly and in good faith" and that he "cannot recall the context or detail of documents" more than 20 years old.
The judge made clear in his 2008 judgement that Tenenbaum's knowledge of the Sibneft-Yugra deal would not have made a difference to his decision, however the leak also suggests some of the documents presented by Abramovich's legal team to the High Court had been falsified.
One of the agreements was dated August 2003, but appears not to have been created or actually signed until 2007.
Abramovich's team had argued in court that Yugraneft's interest had been diluted because of the need for finance for the joint venture.
They claimed Tchigirinsky had approached them "in the spring of 2002" with a view to new financing arrangements. Tchigirinsky denied this was the case.
The leaked documents show that before then, in January 2002, Abramovich's Russian associates had already prepared a bundle of documents.
They included agreements under which two Abramovich companies would acquire shares in Sibneft-Yugra, increasing his stake and diluting Yugraneft's.
This evidence suggests they were already planning to dilute Yugraneft's interest and that the argument they used in court about financing was a smokescreen.
Lawyers for Abramovich said: "The Judgment made no finding that the dilution was premeditated", or that it was "fraudulent". They added: "The Judge found that our client received no property belonging to Yugraneft, and that no Yugraneft asset could be traced into his hands."

articles.title: ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, days after easing sanctions on Russian fuel to tackle soaring domestic and global fuel prices.
The energy truce, announced on Sunday, marks another shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy, as the Iran-US war and recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities disrupted global oil supplies and pushed up fuel prices. Trump has even asked Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, as Moscow remains a major exporter of diesel.
The spike in diesel prices in recent weeks has particularly put pressure on Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections. Surveys show Americans hold the Trump administration responsible for the soaring fuel prices amid the unpopular US war on Iran.
“Attacks on refineries and energy facilities have taken capacity out of an already stretched global fuel market, pushing up costs for transport, agriculture and businesses, with the pain ultimately passed on to consumers,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mutual attacks on energy sites by Ukraine and Russia.
“A genuine ceasefire could help protect supplies and ease some of that pressure, particularly as winter approaches.”
However, she warned it was too early to call it a “diplomatic breakthrough”, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that the energy truce came as a surprise to him.
Trump’s decisions have drawn criticism from US politicians and European allies, who warn that allowing Russian fuel back into global markets could provide Moscow with new revenue to finance its war in Ukraine. In March, the Trump administration gave a sanctions waiver to Russian seaborne oil.
So, why has Trump repeatedly changed his position on Russian energy, and what is behind his latest decisions?
What is the ‘energy ceasefire’ Trump announced?
On Sunday, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.
“Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social, without providing further details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was not aware of the energy truce, saying the deal was “news to me” but welcomed the announcement nonetheless.
However, he said Russian drones continued targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv, after Trump’s statement.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take,” Zelenskyy said on Monday during a video address to a security conference in Warsaw.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, arguing that energy revenues help fund Moscow’s war. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure throughout the four-year conflict.
Academic Alexey Muraviev has urged caution over Trump’s announcement, questioning whether an agreement has actually been reached, and if so, what it entails.
“Is it about suspending attacks on oil refineries? And if that’s the case, then the situation would be inadequate, because Ukraine’s oil refineries have already been taken out by Russia’s strikes beforehand,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
“So, in this sense, it would mean effectively Ukraine suspending unilateral action against Russia’s oil refinery facilities.”
Muraviev also linked the announcement to Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting it may be a signal to Zelenskyy.
“Attacking Russian oil refinery capability would probably be interpreted by Washington as an attack on US economic interests,” he said, referring to the agreement on diesel exports through April 2027.
What’s the state of global oil prices?
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have continued to keep global oil markets under pressure.
On Monday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell to about $103.04 a barrel following Trump’s ceasefire announcement and Russian diesel deal, while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at about $90.96.
However, prices remain elevated because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow.
Recent attacks on Saudi oil installations and airports by Yemen’s Houthis and the fighting around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait have put further pressure on oil prices.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have compounded diesel shortages, affecting a fuel essential for the agriculture and trucking industries.
The crisis prompted the Group of Seven nations last week to agree to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves. The G7 decision came after pressure from Trump.
How has the Trump administration zig-zagged between punishing and embracing Russian energy?
Washington’s approach to Russian energy has shifted repeatedly since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Under President Joe Biden, the US banned Russian oil and energy imports in March 2022, seeking to cut off revenue used to finance Moscow’s war.
But Washington simultaneously supported a G7 price cap on Russian oil, designed to restrict Moscow’s earnings without removing too much supply from global markets.
Moreover, the Biden administration also accepted India’s continued purchases of Russian crude to prevent global prices from rising.
After returning to power last year, Trump initially intensified pressure on Moscow. In August 2025, his administration imposed additional tariffs on Indian goods over New Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil.
Two months later, Washington sanctioned Russian energy giants Rosneft and Lukoil, accusing Moscow of failing to seriously pursue peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
However, Washington’s approach took a dramatic turn this year. On March 5, Washington issued a 30-day waiver allowing India to buy Russian oil stranded at sea, as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid US attacks on Iran threatened global supplies.
A week later, the Trump administration expanded the exemption, allowing countries worldwide to buy sanctioned Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded onto tankers, with the waiver lasting until April 11.
In September, Trump urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, blaming the strikes for global diesel shortages.
On October 9, he announced an agreement with Russian President Putin for Moscow to release more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, with another 1.5 million tonnes to follow.
Why has Trump changed his position on Russian oil frequently?
Trump’s shifting public position on Russian energy reflects ongoing, and often competing, political and economic pressures.
“Trump is caught between his geopolitical ambitions and the domestic political consequences of expensive energy,” Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.
She said Washington was trying to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine while simultaneously allowing Russian fuel sales that could generate additional revenue for the Kremlin.
“The shift may deliver a short-term political gain if supplies increase and prices ease, but it could come at a longer-term diplomatic cost,” she said, adding that the benefits appeared limited while the Middle East war continued.
US diesel prices reached a record $6.52 per gallon in September, placing Trump under pressure ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
However, according to academic Muraviev, the US president’s public rhetoric should be distinguished from his administration’s actions.
“I don’t really see inconsistency in Trump’s approach because, apart from his public rhetoric, apart from his frequent media posting, there’s been a more steady approach on behalf of his administration,” he told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to discussions between Russian and American officials in August and September, suggesting that negotiations over the latest diesel agreement may have begun well before Trump’s announcement last Friday.
Muraviev suggested the timing of the announcement could be politically motivated, allowing Trump to claim a victory on energy prices before the midterms.
Moreover, Moscow also has an interest in helping Trump retain political influence because his administration appears more willing to negotiate with Russia than former President Biden was. Trump has been relatively more accepting of the Russian position on the Ukraine war and has even blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end the war.
“For Putin, it’s not just about scoring immediate economic benefit, but also achieving longer-term political and strategic goals,” Muraviev said, referring to other issues such as Iran, cybersecurity, space cooperation and nuclear arms control.
The energy crisis has also created contrasting consequences for American businesses.
While higher oil prices can boost revenues for US energy producers, they increase operating costs for businesses dependent on fuel.
Susannah Streeter said cheaper diesel could provide relief to trucking companies, farmers and manufacturers, although the additional Russian supplies were unlikely to make a significant difference while disruptions in the Middle East continued.
She also warned that frequent changes to sanctions could create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment and supply-chain decisions.
“If sanctions are relaxed, reimposed or changed at short notice, companies face greater uncertainty over sourcing, compliance and the risk of being caught on the wrong side of a policy reversal,” she said.

articles.title: In Israel’s election, Netanyahu faces a reckoning over Oct. 7 failure - The Forward
articles.summary: In Israel’s election, Netanyahu faces a reckoning over Oct. 7 failure  The ForwardAn Israeli Election Like No Other  The New York TimesBenjamin Netanyahu's legacy and political future on the line in Israel's Oct 27 election  Fox News‘Peace is not in people’s minds’: October 7 scars take center stage for first-time voters  The Times of IsraelIsrael election: Could Naftali Bennett rescue Benjamin Netanyahu from an election deadlock?  The Jerusalem ...
articles.full_text:
Two weeks before Israelis vote, Netanyahu’s former aides deliver explosive testimony, allegations of falsified records and demands for an independent inquiry.
With barely two weeks remaining before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, the country has been consumed by an extraordinary confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior former aides over what he knew before the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7, 2023, what he did with that knowledge and whether his office subsequently sought to rewrite the historical record.
The immediate catalyst was a bombshell television interview in recent days with Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, Netanyahu’s former military secretary, who served alongside him before and during the attack that killed approximately 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Gil had remained largely silent for three years, expecting to present his evidence to a state commission of inquiry. But with Netanyahu blocking such an inquiry, amid transparent scheming to deflect blame, Gil decided to speak publicly.
What he described went considerably beyond the failures of intelligence and military preparedness that have already been extensively documented. Gil accused Netanyahu’s office of attempting to falsify an official record from the morning of the attack. He challenged the prime minister’s account of early warnings he received. He confirmed that Netanyahu rejected recommendations for preventive military operations against Hamas. And he described how political considerations influenced decisions over hostage negotiations, potentially prolonging the captivity of people who could have been brought home earlier – and alive.
His testimony is particularly consequential because it directly challenges a 55-page document Netanyahu released in February, presenting his version of the events preceding Oct. 7. Submitted to Israel’s state comptroller, the document portrayed Netanyahu as having repeatedly advocated tougher action against Hamas while security officials underestimated the threat. It has become central to his defense against accusations that his longstanding policy of containing Hamas helped create the conditions for the catastrophe.
Gil, who attended the relevant meetings and recorded his experiences in 16 notebooks, described the published document as a profoundly incomplete and misleading account, containing lies and half-truths. It failed to reflect even half of what he witnessed.
A separate investigation published Friday by Yedioth Ahronoth, comparing Netanyahu’s account with original records of security deliberations, reported significant omissions and distortions, including instances in which Netanyahu allegedly rejected proposals to target Hamas leaders that his February document presented as initiatives of his own.
Most explosive was Gil’s account of an alleged attempt by Netanyahu’s then-chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, to change the official time of a telephone conversation on Oct. 7 from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. Moving the time backward could create the impression that Netanyahu had been issuing instructions from the first moments of the assault. Gil said a stenographer told him she had been instructed to alter the record, prompting him to notify the attorney general.
Nitzan Alon, another retired general who headed the government’s hostage release operation, and took part in negotiations throughout much of the war, also told reporters that “it was possible to end the war a year earlier” and save the lives of numerous hostages who eventually died in captivity.
Another remarkable confrontation involves Ronen Bar, the former head of the Shin Bet domestic security agency, whom Netanyahu has repeatedly blamed for the failures of Oct. 7. In late September, Bar announced plans to sue Netanyahu for defamation, accusing him of conducting a campaign of false allegations about his conduct before the massacre. Bar said he had warned Netanyahu about a looming security disaster and demanded disclosure of the original records of security meetings, communications and warnings, including the prime minister’s contacts with foreign officials.
Those demands have acquired additional significance amid reports that senior officials from Egypt and the United Arab Emirates warned Netanyahu about Hamas preparations shortly before the attack. Netanyahu categorically denies receiving such warnings and has threatened legal action over the reporting.
Gil’s revelations arrived alongside another striking intervention from a former Netanyahu confidant. Yoav Horowitz, , once Netanyahu’s chief of staff and director-general of the Prime Minister’s Office, told Kan’s Reshet Bet radio last week that he had gradually come to understand that Netanyahu’s decisions were driven primarily by considerations of personal political survival rather than the national interest.
Now a senior aide to leading opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot, Horowitz attributed that transformation to the corrosive effects of prolonged power, observing that “too much time in power corrupts,” and framed the approaching election as being about saving the country.
Horowitz now heads the team preparing its first 100 days in government. His criticism therefore comes from a former trusted aide who has become an active political opponent, adding another dimension to the dispute over Netanyahu’s leadership.
The question of political survival also figured prominently in Gil’s account of the hostage negotiations. Asked whether coalition pressures had influenced decisions that delayed agreements to free hostages, Gil said some hostages could have returned earlier and that political calculations had played a role in the decisions that kept them in captivity.
Netanyahu has rejected Gil’s allegations, and his Likud party has characterized the latest revelations as politically motivated propaganda. Netanyahu and his supporters maintain that senior security officials failed to recognize the imminent danger.
The country is still struggling to establish a common factual account of its most traumatic day in decades, while the officials who participated in the crucial decisions offer sharply conflicting versions of what happened. Meanwhile, the families of those killed on Oct. 7, survivors of the massacre and former hostages continue demanding answers about the decisions that shaped their lives.
The public appetite for an inquiry into the disaster is overwhelming. A September 2025 survey by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 74 percent of Israelis supported establishing a state commission of inquiry, including 68 percent of Jewish respondents identifying with the political right. A subsequent survey conducted in February 2026 found that 92 percent of Israelis considered it important to investigate the events.
The absence of such an inquiry has left journalists, former officials, politicians and bereaved families conducting an increasingly contentious public investigation of their own. Documents appear selectively, witnesses offer competing recollections, and allegations that might otherwise be tested through sworn testimony and access to classified evidence become weapons in an election campaign. With spiraling suspicions being leveled at Netanyahu, the election will take place amid unresolved questions – and a rage that grows more toxic by the day.

articles.title: The Iraq-Syria oil pipeline: Who is behind the project raising conflict-of-interest concerns? - نون بوست
articles.summary: The Iraq-Syria oil pipeline: Who is behind the project raising conflict-of-interest concerns?  نون بوست
articles.full_text:
A project to link Iraq’s oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast is moving forward amid efforts to redraw oil export routes in the Middle East, at an estimated cost of at least $15 billion. It is driven by Baghdad’s need to reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, Damascus’s desire to restore its role in regional energy trade, and US interest in expanding infrastructure investment in both countries.
But the project has raised questions about conflicts of interest following revelations of commercial and financial ties between Thomas Barrack, the US ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Iraq and Syria, and Ziad Ghandour, a businessman who founded the US firm TI Capital.
A Reuters investigation published on 9 October 2026 highlighted the relationship and the legal questions it raises. The US State Department said Barrack was complying with ethics rules and denied that he had any financial interest in the pipeline.
The investors include a consortium led by a Qatari company and involving two US firms, while talks are under way for a major French group to join. Studies into the project’s financing, ownership and operation continue amid financial, security and technical challenges that could mean it takes years to implement.
From Barrack to Ghandour: A network of interests behind the oil project
The Reuters investigation found that Thomas Barrack encouraged TI Capital, founded by Ziad Ghandour, to become involved in a project to transport Iraqi oil to Syria’s Baniyas port. It cited three people familiar with efforts concerning the project, including two sources with direct knowledge of discussions with Iraqi and Syrian officials.
Barrack, an American businessman who founded the investment firm Colony Capital, has business ties with Ghandour dating back years before he took up his diplomatic post.
Documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in March 2021 showed that the two men co-founded Falcon Acquisition, which sought to raise $250 million through an initial public offering. Barrack chaired its board, while Ghandour was its chief executive.
The company’s plans faltered after Barrack was arrested in July 2021 on charges related to acting on behalf of the UAE without registering under US law. A US jury acquitted him in November 2022. The acquisition company partnership ended, but Barrack retained other financial interests in a project managed by Ghandour’s company.
In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, Barrack acknowledged retaining an interest in ACD-TI Oakley Investment, which is linked to a real estate project in Oakley, California, and managed by Ghandour’s company. Under the arrangement, he is entitled to receive 20 per cent of profits above a 15 per cent return threshold in exchange for services he previously provided to the company. He also disclosed that he provided it with advisory services during 2024.
In an ethics agreement signed on 7 March 2025, Barrack pledged to refrain from personal and substantial participation in government matters that directly and predictably affect his financial interests, unless he receives a legal waiver or a regulatory exception applies.
Ghandour has been arranging energy investments for more than two decades. US documents from 2003 and 2004 showed that his company contracted with the US energy firm Centroleum to help arrange negotiations with international companies, including Saudi Aramco and Spain’s Repsol. The agreements included financial arrangements tied to shares and financing.
Efforts concerning the Iraq-Syria oil project date back to May 2026, when Barrack floated the idea of involving Ghandour’s company during a meeting on the sidelines of the Milken Global Conference in Los Angeles. The two men also took part in a closed session on the need to develop new routes for energy supplies in the Middle East.
On 16 June, TI Capital was named in a statement issued by Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi. They praised progress towards signing a memorandum of understanding with the company to revive the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline. An announcement in July then unveiled a broader consortium that included US-based Chevron and Qatar’s UCC.
These developments show how the relationship between Barrack and Ghandour evolved from an investment partnership and financial interests to the diplomatic efforts that preceded Ghandour’s company joining the pipeline project.
Reuters quoted a person close to Barrack as saying the US envoy trusts Ghandour’s ability to help implement the strategy of President Donald Trump’s administration to draw Iraq and Syria closer to the US.
These efforts have raised questions among government ethics experts. Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer and a law professor at the University of Minnesota, said Barrack’s relationship with Ghandour poses a serious problem under federal rules governing the impartiality of government employees. He argued that the US envoy should recuse himself entirely from discussions of the project.
Don Fox, former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, also said that a government official promoting a company with which he has a business relationship could violate rules barring the use of public office to endorse private entities.
US federal ethics rules govern officials’ participation in matters involving people or companies with whom they have business or personal relationships that could cast doubt on their impartiality. The rules also allow the relevant government authority to assess such cases and grant permission to participate.
A records request filed by Reuters showed that the US Office of Government Ethics had no waiver on record concerning Barrack’s participation in the project in light of his relationship with Ghandour’s company. The State Department, however, said Barrack has no stake, role or financial interest in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline. It said his actions are consistent with US policy encouraging regional integration in the energy sector and stressed his compliance with ethics rules.
Ghandour’s company also appeared in a consortium studying the development of the Akkas gas field in Anbar province, alongside UCC and the US oil company ConocoPhillips, according to the Reuters investigation. TI Capital’s website also lists its involvement in projects linked to Syria’s Tartus port.
The consortium and financing: Who will own and operate the pipeline?
On 4 July 2026, the Iraqi cabinet approved authorising the state-owned Basra Oil Co. to sign a preliminary agreement on principles and a non-disclosure agreement with a consortium including TI Capital, Chevron and UCC. The agreements cover technical and financial studies for two proposed oil export routes: one to Türkiye’s Ceyhan port and the other to Syria’s Baniyas port, through a network starting in Basra and passing through Anbar province.
The Iraqi government’s decision said the agreements concern preparing studies and assessing routes, while negotiations continue over the final financial and contractual commitments. The cabinet also approved completing an advisory contract with the US engineering services company KBR for the Basra-Haditha line inside Iraq.
On 17 July, the Iraqi and Syrian governments signed a memorandum of understanding to develop the oil corridor at a ceremony hosted by the US Chamber of Commerce in Washington. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi attended, alongside officials from both countries and representatives of the participating companies.
The signing took place during a visit in which more than 50 agreements, memorandums of understanding and partnerships were announced, worth more than $60 billion in total, according to a US Chamber of Commerce statement issued on 18 July.
The following day, the investor consortium announced that it had signed separate agreements on principles with the two governments through three business entities: Qatar’s UCC OrbaCon for Investment in Concessions, Chevron Business Development for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Tech Infra 2, affiliated with the TI Capital Group.
According to the statement, UCC is coordinating the consortium, while the companies prepare technical and financial feasibility studies and an initial financing plan. A joint Iraqi-Syrian working group is also being formed to address cross-border issues. Ownership stakes, operating rights, transit fees and concession periods remain subject to the completion of negotiations and government approvals.
A prominent member of the consortium is Qatar’s UCC Holding, part of Power International Holding. Its chairman is Qatari businessman Moataz Al Khayyat, while his brother Ramez serves as chief executive.
The company has expanded its investments in Syria. In May 2025, the Syrian government signed a memorandum of understanding with a UCC-led consortium to develop power generation projects, with announced investments of about $7 billion. Thomas Barrack attended the signing ceremony in Damascus.
In November that year, final concession agreements were signed with a consortium led by the company to develop, expand and operate Damascus International Airport. The announced investments totalled about $4 billion and involved Turkish and American companies, as part of UCC’s expansion into Syrian infrastructure projects.
Chevron, one of the largest US oil and gas companies, is participating in the corridor’s preliminary studies as part of its broader interest in Iraq’s oil sector, including negotiations over the development of the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah fields.

articles.summary: Pakistan Petroleum Minister Visits Saudi Arabia for Energy Talks Amid Supply Crisis  Energy Update
articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: Federal Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik arrived in Saudi Arabia on Saturday to attend a high-level international energy conference as Pakistan grapples with rising fuel prices, disrupted liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies and mounting pressure to control subsidies.
Malik is scheduled to participate in the 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial in Riyadh, which is hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria. The meeting brings together officials from major energy-producing and consuming countries, alongside executives from leading energy companies, including Saudi Aramco, ExxonMobil, Shell and BP.
Rabia Khalid, a spokesperson for the petroleum ministry, confirmed Malik’s arrival to Arab News, saying the minister would participate in the conference beginning Sunday.
According to the agenda, Malik is scheduled to speak during a session on investment and trade in sustainable energy solutions, focusing on making energy cleaner, more accessible and affordable.
His visit comes as Pakistan faces mounting energy supply challenges linked to the US-Iran conflict, which has disrupted LNG shipments from Qatar and increased the cost of energy imports. Petrol and diesel prices have risen sharply since the conflict began in late February, approaching Rs400 per litre.
QatarEnergy, a major LNG supplier to Pakistan under long-term agreements, has extended its suspension of deliveries until November 5. The disruption has forced Islamabad to seek alternative supplies ahead of winter, when household demand for natural gas typically increases.
The shortage has also raised concerns about electricity generation. Karachi’s power utility, K-Electric, warned that it could be forced to impose power cuts during evening and nighttime peak hours because of limited supplies of regasified LNG used in power generation.
Rising fuel costs have also complicated the government’s efforts to balance consumer relief with its commitments under the $7 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme.
Last month, Islamabad introduced a fuel relief scheme offering discounted petroleum products to eligible motorcycle riders, rickshaw operators and small-car owners. However, the IMF has urged the government to phase out the programme, citing its fiscal cost and broad coverage.
The government has continued the scheme despite the lender’s concerns over the financial burden of fuel subsidies amid rising international energy prices.
Meanwhile, Pakistan and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement on Wednesday that could unlock approximately $1.2 billion in financing, subject to approval by the lender’s executive board. The IMF also highlighted the economic risks arising from the conflict in the Middle East.
Malik’s participation in the Riyadh meeting provides an opportunity for Pakistan to engage with international energy stakeholders on supply security, investment and sustainable energy solutions as the country seeks to manage import costs and reduce the impact of energy disruptions on consumers and the wider economy.

articles.title: 2026 global market impact on Israeli business - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: 2026 global market impact on Israeli business  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Israel’s economy has always punched above its weight, but the last few years have reshaped how global investors view the Start-Up Nation. Foreign capital flows, currency fluctuations, and shifting trade alliances now dictate everything from Tel Aviv office rents to the price of a hummus lunch in Jerusalem. The connection between international markets and local business decisions grows tighter with every quarterly earnings report. For entrepreneurs and investors tracking these trends, understanding the global-local link is no longer optional. Some savvy investors even diversify their portfolios with entertainment options like Lucky Hills casino canada while monitoring these macroeconomic shifts. That blend of risk management and leisure reflects a broader truth: Modern business success demands both analytical rigor and smart stress relief.
The numbers tell a compelling story about this interdependence. When the U.S. Federal Reserve adjusts interest rates, Israeli tech valuations react within hours. When China’s manufacturing data dips, Haifa’s ports feel the ripple. This article examines the specific channels through which global markets influence Israel’s business environment, offering actionable insights for those navigating this complex landscape.
Key facts: Five numbers that explain the shift
The following statistics illustrate the depth of global-market influence on Israeli business. Each figure represents a data point from credible sources, including the Bank of Israel, the IMF, and the OECD.
- In 2026, foreign direct investment into Israeli high-tech firms reached $28.4 billion, a 17% increase from 2024, driven primarily by U.S. and European venture capital funds.
- The shekel appreciated 9.3% against the dollar between January 2025 and March 2026, forcing exporters to hedge aggressively and reshaping profit margins for manufacturers.
- Israel’s technology sector now accounts for 54% of total exports, up from 48% in 2022, making the economy more sensitive to global tech cycles than ever before.
- Global inflation pressures in 2025 pushed the Bank of Israel to raise interest rates to 5.25%, the highest level since 2006, directly impacting small business lending.
- Trade with Asia, particularly India and South Korea, grew 22% in 2025, reducing Israel’s traditional reliance on European and American partners.
Why currency markets dictate local business strategy
Currency volatility creates winners and losers across Israel’s business landscape. Exporters in the chemical, agricultural, and cybersecurity sectors watch the shekel-dollar exchange rate with religious devotion. A strong shekel hurts their competitiveness, while a weak one boosts overseas revenue. In 2025, the shekel’s unexpected strength squeezed profit margins for many traditional exporters, forcing them to innovate or lose market share.
Meanwhile, importers and domestic retailers benefit from a stronger currency. Consumer electronics, vehicles, and luxury goods become cheaper, which explains why Tel Aviv showrooms expanded their inventories in early 2026. The real estate market also feels these effects. International buyers, particularly from the U.S. and France, purchase properties when the shekel weakens, driving up prices in prime neighborhoods. This dynamic creates an interesting paradox: Global currency markets influence whether a young Israeli couple can afford an apartment in Ra'anana or must look to the periphery.
Technology investments: The global venture capital engine
Venture capital flows represent the most visible connection between global markets and Israel’s business environment. When U.S. tech stocks rally, Israeli start-ups receive more funding. When they stumble, the funding taps tighten. The 2025 artificial intelligence boom, for instance, funneled record amounts into Israeli AI companies. Cybersecurity firms also attracted substantial capital, with investors showing strong confidence in Israel’s proven track record in this domain.
This dependency creates both opportunity and fragility. Israeli start-ups often structure their operations around U.S. market access, hiring American sales teams and establishing Delaware holding companies. The global nature of this funding means local businesses must maintain international standards from day one. Accounting practices, data privacy compliance, and corporate governance all align with U.S. and European norms. This standardization helps Israeli companies scale globally but also exposes them to regulatory changes abroad. The European Union’s Digital Markets Act, for example, forced several Israeli tech firms to redesign their compliance frameworks in 2025, costing millions but ultimately strengthening their market positions.
Trade alliances and geopolitical market shifts
Global trade patterns continuously reshape Israel’s business environment through new agreements and shifting partnerships. The Abraham Accords opened markets in the UAE, Morocco, and Bahrain, creating fresh opportunities for Israeli exporters and investors. Trade with the Gulf states grew 35% in 2025, with technology, agriculture, and water management leading the way. These relationships provide economic diversification that buffers Israel against volatility in traditional markets.
Simultaneously, Israel has deepened ties with Asian economies. India’s growing tech sector partners with Israeli start-ups on everything from agricultural technology to defense systems. South Korea’s semiconductor industry relies on Israeli chip design expertise. These partnerships reduce dependence on any single market, spreading risk across multiple geographies. For local businesses, this means learning new cultural norms, adapting products for different regulatory environments, and building supply chains that span continents. The payoff comes in resilience, but the learning curve remains steep.
The global debt market and local borrowing costs
International bond markets directly influence how Israeli businesses access capital. When global investors perceive Israel as a stable investment, they buy government bonds, driving yields down. This lowers borrowing costs for the entire economy. In 2025, Israel issued a record $12 billion in international bonds, with demand exceeding supply by a factor of three. This strong appetite reflected investor confidence in Israel’s economic fundamentals despite regional tensions.
Corporate borrowers benefit from this dynamic through lower interest rates on business loans and credit lines. Small and medium enterprises, which employ over 60% of Israel’s workforce, gain access to capital that fuels expansion. Conversely, global market turbulence raises borrowing costs, forcing businesses to delay investments or seek alternative funding sources. The 2026 tech correction, for example, pushed some start-ups toward private credit funds and strategic corporate investors rather than traditional bank loans. This shift diversifies Israel’s financial ecosystem, making it more resilient but also more complex.
Practical steps for navigating global market influences
Business leaders in Israel must adopt concrete strategies to thrive in this interconnected environment. First, monitor global macroeconomic indicators weekly, not quarterly. Interest rate decisions from the Federal Reserve, inflation data from the Eurozone, and commodity price movements all provide early signals about future conditions. Second, build currency hedging strategies that protect against unexpected shekel movements. Financial instruments like forward contracts and options cost money but prevent catastrophic losses. Third, diversify export markets to reduce dependency on any single region. Companies that expanded into Asia and the Gulf states weathered the 2025 European slowdown far better than those focused exclusively on the EU.
Fourth, maintain strong relationships with international investors and partners. These connections provide capital during downturns and market intelligence during expansions. Fifth, invest in compliance and governance standards that meet global expectations. This preparation makes Israeli companies attractive to international partners and reduces friction when entering new markets. Finally, embrace flexibility in business planning. The global economy moves quickly, and companies that adapt their strategies rapidly outperform those that stick rigidly to annual plans.
Conclusion
Global markets now function as the primary engine driving Israel’s business environment. Currency fluctuations, international investment flows, trade alliances, and global debt markets all shape local decisions in ways that were unimaginable two decades ago. This interdependence brings both opportunities and challenges. Smart business leaders understand that they cannot control global forces, but they can prepare for them. By monitoring international trends, diversifying across markets, and maintaining flexible strategies, Israeli companies can turn global volatility into competitive advantage. The future belongs to those who read the global tea leaves accurately and act decisively.

Synopsis
Iran's Supreme National Security Council head, Mohsen Rezaei, has called the US response to negotiations insufficient. He warned of potential attacks on cables and data centers if fighting escalates further. In Israel, the former attorney general testified against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a longstanding corruption trial. Meanwhile, the Iranian-backed Houthis claimed responsibility for recent strikes on Saudi airports amid rising tensions.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran says latest US response is 'insufficient'
The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States "insufficient" as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along.
The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.
Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear.
Iran's delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation.
Rezaei also threatened "cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region" if intense fighting breaks out again.
Meanwhile, the Guard's navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be "identified as hostile," according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran's proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday.
Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case
Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial.
Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister.
Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022.
Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes
A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday's attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously" about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace.
The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.
Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue
Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before.
Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee.
"Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes," Abed said.
Israel's military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers.
One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes.
Netanyahu wants probe into 'NAZA' documentary
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary "NAZA," in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza.
Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells "a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel" and its military.
The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel's actions in the Palestinian territory has grown.
Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue.
Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling
Lebanon's army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater.
It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was "directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank" and called it "a flagrant violation of existing understandings."
An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident.
Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March.

A recent alleged plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and "almost certainly directed" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday.
The incident near RAF Fairford began in the early hours of Sept. 27 when five British men in their 20s were arrested near the base on suspected terrorism and explosive offences.
They were later released without charge on police bail "under stringent conditions," and police said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved.
Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from the air base, and U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham told parliament.
"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."
Later on Monday, Iran denied any involvement in the incident at the air base, which has been used by the U.S. in its war with the Islamic republic.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
