articles.title: Finland calls on EU states to stop issuing Russian tourist visas
articles.summary: Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen called on fellow EU member states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Moscow ends its war in Ukraine. Elina Valtonen u...
articles.full_text:
Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen called on fellow EU member states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Moscow ends its war in Ukraine.
Elina Valtonen urged the European Commission to adopt stricter guidelines for processing Russian visa applications and proposed legislative changes needed to implement a complete tourist visa ban, the Finnish Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas," she said.
"Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is now in its fifth year. It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians."
Valtonen said the number of tourist visas issued to Russians by Schengen countries had risen in recent years, with nearly half a million granted in 2025.
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022," Valtonen said.
"The same must finally happen at the EU level."
Valtonen invited other EU member states to join a letter to the European Commission calling for the ban.
The letter also proposes banning Schengen visas for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle and introducing visa restrictions for Russian athletes.
It further calls for an effective implementation of a visa ban on current and former Russian combatants agreed by EU member states this summer, according to the statement.
At 1,343 kilometers (834 miles), Finland has the longest border of any European Union member state with Russia.
The Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939. The Winter War, as it is known, lasted for over three months and despite heavy losses, the USSR won.

articles.title: Musk appears to be biggest-known donor ahead of US miderm elections
articles.summary: Elon Musk, the world's only trillionaire, has spent roughly $366 million on the 2026 midterm elections so far, becoming the biggest known donor as he tried to help Republicans to r...
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk, the world's only trillionaire, has spent roughly $366 million on the 2026 midterm elections so far, becoming the biggest known donor as he tried to help Republicans to retain control of Congress, U.S. media reported on Monday.
Musk has spent about $276 million since July only, even as Democrats' chances of retaking the U.S. House and Senate have improved.
Musk's largess, which was reported earlier by the New York Times (NYT), makes the world's richest person likely the single-biggest political donor in this year's races, according to campaign finance records.
There is a lot at stake for Musk with House Democrats calling for investigations into his government contracts as CEO of aerospace company SpaceX, as well as his work running the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) under President Donald Trump.
The numbers, first reported by the NYT ahead of this week's federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk's super PAC.
The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times.
Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024.
Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk's efforts.
It's a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending . "I think I've done enough," he said at the time.
Musk's net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.
He spent roughly $290 million during the last election cycle.

articles.title: US federal agents search home of Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of probe
articles.summary: U.S. federal agents searched on Monday the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Muslim lawmaker for the state of Minnesota and frequent target of Trump administration criticism, a...
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal agents searched on Monday the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Muslim lawmaker for the state of Minnesota and frequent target of Trump administration criticism, as part of a criminal investigation, media reports said.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents conducted the search, said the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke to The Associated Press (AP) on the condition of anonymity.
More details about the investigation were not immediately clear, although Vice President JD Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud – an allegation she has denied – and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.
The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area, but provided no other details. The street was blocked off on Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the department said.
The raid followed a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child, Fox News Digital reported, citing unidentified sources.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department.
Omar represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She was first elected to the House in 2018 and has been a member of what's called The Squad of female lawmakers known for their progressive views and pointed opposition to President Donald Trump, a Republican.
Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies."
"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May.
"So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime."
In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America."
He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and "trying to look at what the remedies are."
"That’s the thing that we’re trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she’s committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?”
Omar’s office in March dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
"This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to ‘create stories’ to redirect the media,” Omar’s chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement.
"This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party’s unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers," McNutt said of the vice president’s allegations and comments.
Omar, an outspoken critic of Trump, has called his focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
Last week, Trump also criticized the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticized the Republican president's rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage."
Trump in February said that Omar and Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."
Both lawmakers had criticized Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration's hard-line immigration crackdown and its immigration enforcement actions.
There was no immediate public response from Omar to Monday's search.
No charges were announced in connection with the search.

articles.title: French student protesters mull fresh demos to maintain momentum
articles.summary: French high school students Monday were planning a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions and launch wave of demonstrations to maintain momentum. The new protests, sch...
articles.full_text:
French high school students Monday were planning a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions and launch wave of demonstrations to maintain momentum.
The new protests, scheduled for Tuesday, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down.
On Friday, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country's lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.
More than 96% were opening Friday, said the Education Ministry.
The authorities are all the more keen to see the student protests end given that online activists have called for demonstrations next Saturday to protest the cost of living.
For President Emmanuel Macron's administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement.
Their protests, launched in 2018 over a planned fuel tax rise, saw massive demonstrations and clashes between police and protesters that shook the presidency during Macron's first term in office.
The government is still counting the cost of the high school protests.
A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was "at least 30 million euros."
On Friday, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86% of them minors.
After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand.
Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students' demands.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu Sunday promised to make changes to the planned budget 2027 to respond to some demands set out in an online platform the government set up to gather students' views.
The student organizations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however.
The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as "crumbs." They are maintaining their demand for an extra 10 million euros to be invested in the country's lycees.
France's 10,000 medical students, however, are beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams starting Monday that help determine their eventual speciality.
They do not want to see the students' action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.
Last Thursday's student demonstrations mobilized tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to Interior Ministry figures.
Nearly 256,000 took part in last Tuesday's day of action.
And one poll, carried out by Ipsos-BVA and published Sunday, said 54% of respondents backed the high school student protests.
They had the most sympathy with student complaints about the excessive size of classes and with the need to renovate the country's crumbling schools.

articles.title: Trump's energy truce claim baffles Kyiv as Russian strikes continue
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia continues to strike Ukraine's energy facilities, despite President Donald Trump's claim a day earlier that both nati...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia continues to strike Ukraine's energy facilities, despite President Donald Trump's claim a day earlier that both nations had agreed to an energy cease-fire.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy cease-fire deal with Russia which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same.
"We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's brief social media post Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy cease-fire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"
Yet Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been "horribly surprised" that following Trump's "sudden but very important post," Russia had struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.
"It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has leveled strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, prompting Trump to blame Zelenskyy for high diesel prices on world markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel in an attempt to address high fuel prices just weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy cease-fire this winter, "we will respond."
"We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. "This energy cease-fire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war."
The European Union's top diplomat Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
"Personally, I would also welcome that the cease-fire would include people not being killed, not only energy," she added.
Ukrainian and European officials reacted with dismay to Trump's diesel deal with Putin, saying it will help fund Russia's war effort.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told reporters in Luxembourg Monday that he doesn't believe the deal "is actually going to change anything" in terms of fuel prices and that it is "much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S."
Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a cease-fire.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night.
"Under such circumstances, it's impossible to hold elections," he said, but added that he would be ready to work toward doing so if Ukraine secured a full cease-fire lasting at least 60 days.
A Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office.
Investigators said the attack occurred at approximately 7:25 p.m., striking a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores and sparking a fire.
Ukrainian air defense forces shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones overnight Monday, Ukraine's Air Force said in a Telegram post.
The attack involved one Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and 121 drones, including 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, the statement said.
Strikes were recorded at 15 locations in Ukraine, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
The Russian Defense Ministry Monday said its air defenses overnight intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions as well as the illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
In a separate statement, the ministry said its forces overnight carried out drone strikes on Ukraine's unspecified port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Ukraine's port city of Odesa with military cargo on board.
